transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-10-05
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Brooks (Redwood SE), Leah Cortes (CTO, HorizonAI), Priya Rao (ML Lead), Ivan Mendez (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Quick review of pilot economics: tokens/sec/$, batching vs latency, and caching savings.
- Discussed three config scenarios: hosted, dedicated, private (VPC).
- Agreed to run KV cache stress test and produce updated cost scenarios.
- Next steps: Samir to send pricing sheet, Maya to run benchmarks, HorizonAI to share traces.

Topics:
- tokens per dollar math and assumptions
- batching latency tradeoffs (50ms vs 250ms windows)
- prefix/KV caching observed savings (~20-35%)
- quantization/precision impact on throughput and quality
- security: SOC2, KMS, VPC peering

===== Transcript =====
[00:00] Samir Patel: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Samir from Redwood, I'm on with Maya our systems SE. How's everybody doing?
[00:06] Leah Cortes: Good, thanks Samir. Busy week but excited to see the numbers.
[00:10] Priya Rao: Hi, thanks. We pushed an updated prompt set yesterday, hope that got into the run.
[00:15] Maya Brooks: Yep we ran it overnight. Quick note — a couple prompts had very long prefixes so the KV cache hit rate changed a bit, I can show the breakdown.
[00:25] Ivan Mendez: Quick ask up front, we're still balancing a 95th percentile latency SLO of 300ms for inference across user-facing calls — want to make sure any batching doesn't push us over.
[00:33] Samir Patel: Totally understood, so today's goal: review tokens/sec per dollar with current pilot runs, look at caching numbers and the batching tradeoffs, and define a short action plan.

[00:50] Maya Brooks: Ok diving in — we ran three main configs last night: (1) default hosted with small batch window (50ms), (2) larger batch window 200ms to maximize throughput, (3) dedicated GPU with int8 quant where applicable.
[01:05] Priya Rao: Wait, Maya, when you say int8 quant, did you test the accuracy drop on the generation length we use? We saw a small hallucination bump in our initial local tests.
[01:14] Maya Brooks: Good call—we did a quick eval against your pass/fail prompt set. Quality delta was minimal on the shorter responses you mostly use — maybe 0.8 to 1.2% of responses flagged for review. Longer chain-of-thought prompts did degrade a bit.
[01:30] Leah Cortes: That's useful. So for our chat summarization flow (short-form) quant looks promising. But for 'compose' feature we might need higher precision.

[01:48] Maya Brooks: Right — so in terms of tokens per dollar: hosted small-batch scenario averaged about 3,400 tokens per dollar for your mixed workload. Large-batch increased to ~5,500 tokens per dollar but added median latency about +60ms and 95th went up roughly +120ms. Dedicated + int8 pushed to ~7,200 tokens per dollar, 95th latency back down to acceptable because of higher throughput on GPU.
[02:10] Ivan Mendez: Can you translate that to tokens/sec per dollar? We budgeted for tokens/sec/$ in our cost model.
[02:16] Maya Brooks: Sure — rough numbers: small-batch hosted was ~45 tokens/sec per dollar, large-batch ~72 tokens/sec/$, dedicated quant ~95 tokens/sec/$. Those are based on the pilot traffic profile you provided.
[02:32] Priya Rao: Hmm 95 tokens/sec/$ sounds great, but what's the per-request latency distribution there? If 95th is 900ms that's not viable.
[02:40] Maya Brooks: For dedicated quant the median latency was 85ms, 95th around 260ms in our runs — that's within your 300ms SLO. On the large-batch hosted, the 95th was edging to 420ms for spike requests.

[02:58] Samir Patel: Important nuance — large batching helps when requests arrive at a steady cadence. If you have bursty traffic batching window will fill unpredictably and tail latency suffers.
[03:12] Leah Cortes: Our traffic is bursty during feature releases; the cadence isn't stable. Could caching help mitigate that?
[03:19] Maya Brooks: Yes — prefix/KV caching gave us a 28% token reduction on average across your prompt set. For repeated system prompts and context reuse we saw hit rates up to 46% on certain routes. That means fewer tokens generated and lower cost, plus improved latency for cache hits.
[03:38] Ivan Mendez: That 46% sounds like a best-case — what about worst-case?
[03:41] Maya Brooks: Worst-case in the sample was around 12% hit-rate on the 'compose' route where prompts vary a lot. So you should plan per-route cache profiles.
[03:52] Priya Rao: Are there any correctness issues with the cache? Like stale KV or key collision?
[03:57] Maya Brooks: Cache keys are deterministic on the prompt fingerprint and session features. We support TTLs and invalidation hooks so you can evict keys when you roll prompts. We noticed a few edge cases where punctuation changes keys, so we suggest normalizing prompts before hashing.
[04:12] Leah Cortes: Good call. Security question — if we go private deployment, how does KMS work and do you support customer-managed keys?
[04:20] Samir Patel: Yes — private supports customer KMS/HSM. We integrate with common providers (AWS KMS, GCP). On the compliance side Redwood's hosted product is SOC 2, and Private adds audit log retention windows per contract. We'll attach the security deck as requested.

[04:40] Ivan Mendez: Also need SSO/SAML mapping for roles and RBAC so only certain devs can access model rollouts.
[04:46] Maya Brooks: We have SSO integrations and granular RBAC in the console; we can demo role assignments in the next exec demo.

[05:00] Priya Rao: Back to economics — can you break down the per-token cost that produced the tokens/sec/$ numbers? I'm trying to reconcile with our internal compute pricing.
[05:07] Maya Brooks: Sure — it's a combination of per-token runtime compute plus a small infra overhead. For hosted we model per-token execution cost plus service margin; dedicated is a reserved capacity model with an amortized GPU cost. Example: for your pilot on t4-like 24GB equivalent, runtime token cost ~0.000012 USD/token, plus Redwood service layer 0.000003 — totals 0.000015/token which yields the numbers I quoted given throughput.
[05:33] Leah Cortes: Can you produce that as a simple spreadsheet with assumptions? We need to plug it into our finance model.
[05:38] Samir Patel: Absolutely — that is one of the next steps. I'll include three scenarios and sensitivity on traffic patterns.

[05:52] Ivan Mendez: One other operational point: batching windows — can we do adaptive batching that shrinks under burst?
[05:58] Maya Brooks: Yes, we have adaptive batching that reduces batch delay under high concurrency and grows when idle to maximize tokens/sec. It uses a latency target you set. For your 300ms SLO we can tune it to prioritize tail latency and still get some batching benefits.
[06:12] Priya Rao: For the dedicated quant run — any special kernel or runtime flags we should be aware of?
[06:17] Maya Brooks: We used optimized kernels for int8 on Ampere GPUs and tuned attention kernels for shorter sequence lengths. Also enabled KV caching and asynchronous I/O for network hidden state. We'll share the exact config in the artifact bucket.

[06:34] Samir Patel: Quick pause for questions from your side.
[06:37] Leah Cortes: Yes — how do we approach fallback if a dedicated node is saturated? We need graceful degradation.
[06:42] Maya Brooks: Smart routing — requests can failover to a lower-cost hosted variant or a smaller model. You can set per-route policies: prefer dedicated then hosted, and a compatibility matrix ensures consistent outputs. Loss in quality depends on model size but we can configure A/B testing to measure impact.

[07:00] Priya Rao: We'd like one canary model for fallback that matches our main model's behavior closely.
[07:04] Samir Patel: We can recommend variants; we also provide drift monitoring to detect quality regressions during fallbacks.

[07:18] Ivan Mendez: About metrics: can Redwood export token-level billing and latency traces into our observability stack?
[07:23] Maya Brooks: Yes — we push traces to Datadog/Prometheus and can stream token-level events to your pipeline. We also have per-route dashboards in Redwood Console.

[07:35] Leah Cortes: Great. Any surprises in the pilot that you didn't expect?
[07:38] Maya Brooks: Two small surprises: (1) the prompt normalization issue I mentioned — punctuation causing cache misses — simple to fix but had a measurable cost impact. (2) Some of your 'system' messages had variable session tokens which decreased cache hit ratio; if you standardize system prompts you'll increase cache savings materially.

[07:58] Priya Rao: Ok noted. For the next step benchmarks, can we request a 2-hour oriented run that simulates release-day bursts?
[08:05] Maya Brooks: Yes, Maya will run a 2-hour KV cache stress test with a synthetic burst pattern and sweep batch window sizes while collecting 50/95/99 latencies.

[08:18] Samir Patel: I'll also prepare the tokens-per-dollar sheet; note I'll include assumptions about quantization quality delta and per-route cache hit scenarios (pessimistic/expected/optimistic).

[08:30] Ivan Mendez: Timeline wise we need budget sign-off by middle of October. If we get the numbers quickly we can push decision to 10/20.
[08:40] Samir Patel: That aligns; we'll aim to have the artifacts before 10/9.

[08:50] Maya Brooks: One more ops note — if you choose private, the on-prem install requires a maintenance window for initial weights sync. Expect a 2-4 hour window.

[08:59] Leah Cortes: That's fine. Also, on licensing, do we lock model versions or allow rolling updates?
[09:05] Samir Patel: You can pin model versions per-route and control rollouts with canaries. Rollbacks are supported automatically if quality regression alerts trigger.

[09:18] Priya Rao: Can you also include a quick mapping of which routes should be cached vs not? A short recommendation doc would be helpful.

[09:24] Samir Patel: Yes I'll include a per-route recommendation (cache/no-cache) based on our hit-rate analysis.

[09:33] Leah Cortes: Ok let's recap next steps.

[09:36] Samir Patel: Recap: 1) Maya run 2-hour KV cache + batching sweep and upload logs by 10/08. 2) Samir send tokens-per-dollar spreadsheet and scenario pricing by 10/09. 3) HorizonAI to share anonymized request traces by 10/07. 4) Schedule 30-min exec demo w/ role-based demo week of 10/12.

[09:58] Ivan Mendez: Sounds good. Anything else?
[10:01] Priya Rao: No, that's it for me. Thanks all.
[10:04] Maya Brooks: Thanks — we'll follow up in Slack and drop the artifacts in the shared drive.
[10:08] Samir Patel: Thank you everyone, talk soon.


Meeting close.
